reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because it presents technical-support stories about diagnosing a projector and validating a vehicle warranty. The luxury-car segment is used as a warranty example, with the reported resolution being a milk bottle found in an air-conditioning duct. Requests to subscribe and give a thumbs up are ordinary channel engagement, not conditions for payment, investment, credentials, or another transaction.

citations.quote: The projector hasn't been working for a few months, why isn't it fixed?
I've just taken a contract gig to design an IT warranty system for a major, you'd know the name, luxury car manufacturer.
They keep going until they find an empty glass. Milk bottle. In an air conditioning duct.
Thanks for watching and don't forget to give a thumbs up if you enjoyed it.

opening.argument: Judge, consider the invitation as a promise tied to a simple viewer action: “Like this video if you want to see more!” The description also places a subscription link beside that invitation. The offered benefit is more content, and the requested steps are liking and subscribing. That is a low-effort participation pitch, even though the video does not ask for money.

citations.quote: Like this video if you want to see more!
Subscribe! https://bit.ly/2ZA7DRQ

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense calls these ordinary engagement requests, but that does not answer the wording of the like request: it connects an action with seeing more. The absence of a payment request narrows the concern; it does not erase the participation pitch.

citations.quote: Like this video if you want to see more!

true_side_reply.rebuttal: “If you want to see more” expresses interest in future videos, not a promise that liking unlocks a reward. The subscription link likewise offers no claim, verification, payment, or withdrawal flow. The narrated content is a technical-support story, not an offer to acquire an asset or payout.

opening.argument: The description puts an external shortened link directly after “Subscribe!” and follows it with a request to like the video to see more. A judge should scrutinize that combination: the destination is not evident from the link text, while the surrounding copy encourages a quick action for the prospect of more content. The claim is modest, but so is the effort asked of the viewer.

citations.quote: Subscribe! https://bit.ly/2ZA7DRQ
Like this video if you want to see more!

rebuttal.rebuttal: The projector and milk-bottle resolutions establish what the stories discuss, not what the description’s shortened link leads to. Nor does the closing thumbs-up request account for the separate linked subscription prompt. Those story details should not end scrutiny of the viewer-facing invitation.

citations.quote: Subscribe! https://bit.ly/2ZA7DRQ
Thanks for watching and don't forget to give a thumbs up if you enjoyed it.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A shortened subscription link deserves caution, but its destination is not supplied, so a deceptive destination cannot be inferred. The only stated benefit is seeing more videos. Neither the link nor the like request promises cash, an asset, or another claimable reward.

citations.quote: Subscribe! https://bit.ly/2ZA7DRQ
Like this video if you want to see more!

opening.argument: Judge, the technical anecdotes also serve as an audience-acquisition vehicle. The title advertises a luxury-car debugging story, the description asks viewers to subscribe through a link and like the video to see more, and the narration closes by requesting a thumbs-up. Read together, the story supplies the attraction while the surrounding prompts steer viewers toward participation for more content.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense accurately describes the narrated warranty incident, but story content and promotion can coexist. Finding the milk bottle explains the car’s rattle; it does not explain away the separate calls for viewers to like and subscribe. Assess those requests as part of the video’s overall purpose.

Subscribe! https://bit.ly/2ZA7DRQ

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Audience promotion is not, by itself, a scam solicitation. The title and narration present technical-support anecdotes, and the description’s requests concern ordinary engagement with future videos. They do not make access to a reward conditional on taking action.
